title: DOES GOD REALLY HATE DIVORCE MORE THAN THE ABUSE THAT IS DESTROYING YOU INSIDE YOUR MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: DOES GOD REALLY HATE DIVORCE MORE THAN THE ABUSE THAT IS DESTROYING YOU INSIDE YOUR MARRIAGE?

What if the Scripture used to keep you trapped was never meant to protect the person hurting you? A painful, Bible-centered confrontation with marriage, covenant, abuse, religious silence, and the heart of Jesus Christ.
There is a woman sitting in a church pew this Sunday who almost didn't make it there alive.
Her makeup is carefully applied. Her Bible is open. Her children are sitting beside her. When the worship leader begins singing about the goodness of God, she raises her trembling hands.
Nobody notices that her wrists are covered.
Nobody knows that she spent the previous night locked in a bathroom, praying that the man who promised to love her would finally stop screaming.
And nobody knows the question she has been too terrified to ask out loud.
"God, do You hate divorce so much that You would rather watch me be destroyed?"
Somewhere else, a husband is sitting quietly in the back of another church.
He has been humiliated, threatened, financially controlled, isolated from friends, and repeatedly told that no one would believe him if he spoke.
He has heard that a Christian man must lead his household.
But nobody ever explained what to do when the person he loves uses his commitment to marriage as permission to destroy his dignity.
He wonders whether admitting the abuse makes him weak.
He wonders whether leaving would make him unfaithful.
And somewhere between the sermon and the closing prayer, he whispers something he has never dared to say publicly.
"Lord, I don't know how much longer I can survive this."
Now imagine what happens when either of these people finally finds the courage to tell someone.
They sit across from a respected Christian leader, trembling as they describe the threats, the intimidation, the violence, the manipulation, the constant fear.
And before anyone asks whether they are safe, someone opens a Bible and says:
"God hates divorce."
Four words.
Spoken with conviction.
Sometimes spoken with good intentions.
But when those words are used to silence someone experiencing abuse, something terribly wrong has happened.
Because the question is not whether God values marriage.
He does.
The question is whether God values marriage so much that the person being harmed must remain exposed to danger to prove their faithfulness.
And to answer that question, we must do something more courageous than repeating a familiar religious phrase.
We must open the Scriptures, examine what they actually say, and allow Jesus Christ—not fear, tradition, or human control—to have the final authority.
The answer may challenge what some of us have been taught.
But truth is not the enemy of a holy marriage.
Truth is what exposes everything pretending to be holy.
And sometimes the first thing that must be confronted is the way we have handled the Bible itself.
For years, Malachi 2:16 has been quoted as though it settles every conversation about divorce.
"God hates divorce."
But the Hebrew text deserves more careful attention than that.
The Hebrew of Malachi 2:16 begins with the words:
כִּי־שָׂנֵא שַׁלַּח
Ki sane shallach.
The wording is difficult, and English translations differ because interpreters must make decisions about the grammar and context.
The traditional King James Version reads:
"For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away."
The English Standard Version, however, renders the beginning differently:
"For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence."
These are not identical translations.
And that matters.
The Hebrew word shalach carries the sense of sending away or dismissing. In this context, it concerns the dismissal of a wife.
The verb sane means to hate.
But the grammatical question is who is doing the hating and how the statement relates to the husband's actions.
Responsible biblical interpretation must acknowledge that difficulty rather than pretend every translation says precisely the same thing.
Now look at the surrounding passage.
Malachi 2:14 describes a wife as:
אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ
Eshet beritek.
"The wife of your covenant."
The prophet is confronting men who have dealt treacherously with their wives.
These women were not disposable possessions.
They were covenant partners.
God was witnessing how they were being treated.
The passage condemns marital faithlessness and treachery. It is not a divine permission slip for a violent spouse to demand continued access to the person being harmed.
In fact, Malachi 2:16 also contains the Hebrew expression:
חָמָס
Chamas.
The word means violence, wrongdoing, or violent injustice, depending on its context.
The verse speaks of someone covering his garment with violence.
Scholars differ over the exact relationship between this imagery and the divorce language, but the broader moral concern is unmistakable.
God is confronting covenant betrayal.
He is not congratulating the betrayer for remaining legally married while violating the covenant's obligations.
Think about that.
A person can remain married on paper while betraying the covenant through cruelty, intimidation, violence, and persistent unfaithfulness.
A marriage certificate is not proof that someone is behaving faithfully before God.
And a wedding ring cannot make wickedness righteous.
The God who witnesses the marriage covenant also witnesses what happens behind the locked bedroom door.
He sees what the congregation never sees.
He hears the threats whispered where nobody else can hear.
He knows the difference between a difficult marriage and a dangerous one.
And He is not deceived by someone who raises holy hands in public while using those same hands to terrorize a spouse in private.
But perhaps you are thinking:
"Didn't Jesus Himself forbid divorce?"
We need to hear Him carefully.
In Matthew 19, religious leaders approach Jesus with a question about divorce.
"Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?" (Matthew 19:3, ESV)
Notice what they are asking.
They are not asking how to rescue a battered spouse.
They are asking whether a husband can dismiss his wife for virtually any reason.
Jesus responds by returning to God's original design for marriage.
He speaks of the man and woman becoming one flesh.
He declares:
"What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." (Matthew 19:6, KJV)
Marriage is not supposed to be a disposable arrangement.
It is a sacred covenant.
Jesus refuses to trivialize it.
But listen to what He says when the religious leaders appeal to Moses and divorce certificates.
"Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so." (Matthew 19:8, KJV)
In the Greek text, the expression for hardness of heart is:
σκληροκαρδία
Sklerokardia.
It refers to stubbornness or hardness of heart.
Jesus exposes the human sin that makes divorce a reality in a fallen world.
And He identifies sexual immorality as an exception in Matthew 19:9.
Christians differ over how the relevant passages apply to other circumstances, including abandonment and severe abuse.
Some traditions recognize additional grounds for divorce; others permit separation for protection while maintaining narrower grounds for divorce and remarriage.
Those differences should be acknowledged honestly.
What we cannot responsibly do is pretend Jesus was addressing every possible circumstance of domestic violence in Matthew 19.
He was confronting the misuse of divorce and defending the seriousness of marriage.
Protecting marriage from casual betrayal is not the same thing as requiring someone to endure violence.
Jesus never commands a spouse to submit to being beaten, sexually assaulted, threatened, or terrorized.
And we must never manufacture such a command in His name.
Consider another passage.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "love" is:
ἀγαπᾶτε
Agapate.
It is a form of agapao, the verb used here to command husbands to love their wives.
But Paul does not leave that love undefined.
He points to Jesus Christ.
The One who gave Himself.
The One who served.
The One who sacrificed.
The One who laid down His life.
Christian marital love is measured against the self-giving love of Christ.
Not domination.
Not intimidation.
Not sexual coercion.
Not threats.
Not the calculated destruction of another person's confidence.
And certainly not the demand that a spouse suffer in silence so the abusive partner can preserve a respectable reputation.
Ephesians 5:21 also calls believers to submit to one another in reverence for Christ.
Whatever differences Christians have about the interpretation of marital roles, no legitimate interpretation makes cruelty a Christian virtue.
And Colossians 3:19 is unmistakably direct:
"Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them." (KJV)
The Greek command includes:
μὴ πικραίνεσθε
Me pikrainesthe.
"Do not become bitter" or "do not treat them harshly."
The apostle Paul did not command husbands to cultivate harshness.
He prohibited it.
And Scripture's condemnation of violence and oppression extends beyond any single marriage passage.
Psalm 11:5 says:
"The LORD trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth." (KJV)
Read that again.
The Lord hates the love of violence.
So when someone asks, "Does God hate divorce more than abuse?" we must be careful not to turn the question into a contest of which sin God hates most.
Scripture does not provide a simple ranking that allows us to measure every circumstance that way.
But it gives us more than enough reason to reject the claim that preserving the appearance of marriage matters more than protecting someone from violence.
God's holiness does not require the victim to become a sacrifice on the altar of the abuser's reputation.
There is another passage we cannot ignore.
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul addresses marriage, separation, and abandonment.

He writes that a wife should not separate from her husband, and that a husband should not divorce his wife. He also acknowledges circumstances in which separation has occurred (1 Corinthians 7:10–11).
Later, he addresses a situation in which an unbelieving spouse leaves.
In 1 Corinthians 7:15, he writes:
The Greek phrase is:
οὐ δεδούλωται
Ou dedoulotai.
Literally, "has not been enslaved."
Paul is discussing abandonment by an unbelieving spouse.
We should not pretend the verse directly addresses every abusive marriage or automatically resolves every question about divorce and remarriage.
It does not.
Yet it reveals something important about Paul's treatment of marriage.
He does not teach that a believer must exercise absolute control over a departing spouse to preserve the outward form of the relationship.
And he reminds believers that God has called them to peace.
The Greek word is:
εἰρήνῃ
Eirene.
Peace.
Not the false peace of everyone pretending nothing happened.
Not the silence that follows a threat.
Not the temporary calm that exists only because one person is terrified to speak.
Biblical peace is not maintained by hiding evil.
And reconciliation cannot be manufactured by forcing someone back into danger.
There is a difference between forgiveness and restored trust.
There is a difference between repentance and regret over consequences.
There is a difference between a person saying "I'm sorry" and a person demonstrating sustained transformation.
An abuser may cry.
An abuser may quote Scripture.
An abuser may promise that this time will be different.
An abuser may even become visibly religious after being confronted.
But tears are not the same as repentance.
Religious vocabulary is not the same as a changed heart.
And the forgiveness Jesus commands does not require immediate reconciliation, restored access, or the removal of necessary protection.
John the Baptist said:
"Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance." (Matthew 3:8, KJV)
The Greek word for repentance is:
μετάνοια
Metanoia.
It describes repentance, a turning of mind and life.
Biblical repentance is more than a moment of emotion.
It bears fruit.

For an abusive person, meaningful repentance includes taking responsibility without blaming the victim, ending coercive behavior, accepting consequences, respecting boundaries, and demonstrating sustained change.
Professional intervention and accountability may be necessary.
Even genuine repentance does not entitle someone to immediate reconciliation.
Forgiveness cannot be used as a weapon to demand access to the person who was harmed.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading this are not merely studying a theological question.
They are living inside it.
You have learned to recognize footsteps.
You know what a certain expression means before a word is spoken.
You have deleted messages because you were afraid of what would happen if your spouse found them.
You have apologized for things you did not do because you needed the argument to stop.
You have been told that you are too sensitive.
That you are imagining things.
That you are destroying the family.
That nobody else would ever want you.
That your children will blame you.
That God will punish you if you leave.
And perhaps the most devastating words of all:
"A real Christian would forgive me."
So you forgive.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until forgiveness becomes the word someone uses to describe your continued exposure to harm.
But hear this carefully.
Forgiveness is a Christian calling. Enabling continued abuse is not.
You can forgive someone while refusing to give them another opportunity to hurt you.
You can pray for someone's repentance while maintaining physical distance.
You can desire their salvation without surrendering your safety.
You can take marriage seriously while acknowledging that a marriage has become dangerous.
And you can seek help without first obtaining permission from the person harming you.
Abuse is not limited to bruises.
It can include threats, sexual coercion, financial control, isolation, stalking, humiliation, intimidation, and the calculated use of religion to control another person.
Not every disagreement is abuse.
Not every painful marriage is abusive.
But when a pattern of coercion, fear, domination, or violence exists, treating it as ordinary marital conflict can expose the victim to further harm.
And the church must learn the difference.
Because there are people who have walked into church buildings looking for refuge and walked out carrying another burden.
They were told to pray harder.
To submit more.
To stop provoking their spouse.
To remember that marriage is forever.
Sometimes they were sent to couples counseling while the abusive partner continued using intimidation and control.

In situations involving coercive control or violence, ordinary couples counseling can be unsafe because the victim may face retaliation for speaking honestly. Specialized assessment and individual safety planning are often more appropriate.
A church that genuinely honors marriage must also take abuse seriously.
That means listening carefully.
Taking disclosures seriously.
Helping people access appropriate professional and legal protection.
Protecting children.
Avoiding premature pressure to reconcile.
And refusing to confuse a church leader's desire to save a marriage with the actual safety of the people inside it.
Romans 12:9 says:
"Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good." (KJV)
Love does not require us to rename evil as good.
And protecting an abusive person from accountability is not the same as extending grace.
Now consider the Jesus we meet in the Gospels.
In John 8, a woman accused of adultery is brought before Him.
Religious leaders place her in the center of a public confrontation.
They want a judgment.
They want a spectacle.
They want to use her situation to trap Jesus.

The account in John 7:53–8:11 has a well-known textual history: it is absent from some of the earliest Greek manuscripts, and many modern Bibles mark that fact. Christians have long cherished the passage, but we should be transparent about its textual status.
In the traditional account, Jesus refuses to participate in their merciless spectacle.
He confronts the accusers.
And He tells the woman:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)
Grace.
And truth.
Not condemnation without mercy.
Not mercy without moral seriousness.
Jesus does not excuse sin.
But neither does He allow religious people to use another person's brokenness as an opportunity for cruelty.
And in Luke 4:18, Jesus announces His mission in language drawn from Isaiah:
"He hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives..." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "deliverance" is:
ἄφεσις
Aphesis.
It can mean release, liberation, or forgiveness, depending on the context.
Luke's passage speaks of Christ's mission in the fulfillment of God's saving promises. It should not be reduced to a direct statement about divorce.
But it does reveal the character of the Savior.
Jesus is not indifferent to people crushed under oppression.
He is not the patron of cruelty.
He does not delight in human captivity.
And no Christian should invoke His name to make another person easier to exploit.
Perhaps you have been told that leaving an abusive environment means you lack faith.
But faith is not the refusal to recognize danger.
In Matthew 10:23, Jesus tells His disciples that when they are persecuted in one town, they may flee to another.
That passage concerns persecution in ministry, not marital divorce.
Still, it demonstrates that avoiding danger is not inherently a betrayal of faith.
And Proverbs 22:3 says:
"A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished." (KJV)
Wisdom recognizes danger.
Seeking safety is not automatically cowardice.
Sometimes it is precisely what wisdom requires.

If you are in immediate danger, prioritize reaching a safe place and contacting local emergency services. If possible, speak privately with a qualified domestic violence advocate who can help you develop a safety plan. Leaving an abusive relationship can be a particularly dangerous period, so the timing and method of leaving should be planned carefully when circumstances allow.
If children are being harmed or threatened, their safety must be addressed as well.
You do not need to wait until the violence becomes worse to take your fear seriously.
And you do not have to resolve every theological question about divorce and remarriage before protecting yourself from immediate harm.
Those questions deserve careful biblical counsel, but safety cannot be postponed until every disagreement among Christians has been settled.
Now I want to speak to the person who has been carrying an unbearable amount of shame.
Maybe you have already separated.
Maybe your divorce is final.
Maybe you are sitting in church convinced that everyone sees you as a failure.
You look at families worshiping together and wonder what happened to yours.
You hear sermons about covenant and feel something break inside your chest.
You remember the wedding.
The promises.
The photographs.
The prayers.
The future you thought you were building.
And now all you have are memories of a life that did not become what you hoped.
You may still love the person who hurt you.
You may still grieve what happened.
You may still wonder whether you should have done more.
But please hear this.
Grieving a broken marriage does not mean you were wrong to seek safety.
You are allowed to mourn something that was precious to you.
You are allowed to acknowledge that some memories were beautiful while other experiences were devastating.
You are allowed to feel sorrow without interpreting that sorrow as a command to return.
And if you are struggling with guilt, bring it into the light of God's Word rather than surrendering to the accusations of people who do not know your story.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." (KJV)
This is not a declaration that every decision a Christian makes is automatically right.
It is the announcement that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict of sin.
Our hope is not that we have managed every relationship perfectly.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who extends mercy to the brokenhearted.
The One who makes redemption possible.
And this is where we must confront another painful truth.
Some marriages are destroyed not by the person who finally leaves, but by the person who repeatedly violates the covenant.
That does not mean every divorce is justified.
It does not mean abuse automatically answers every question about remarriage.
And it does not mean Christians should stop working toward healthy marriages.
It means responsibility must be assigned truthfully.
The person who exposes abuse is not necessarily the person who caused the destruction.
The person who seeks protection is not necessarily the person who abandoned faithfulness.
And the person who insists on preserving the marriage's public appearance is not necessarily the person honoring God.
A covenant is not honored merely because two people remain under the same roof.
It is honored through faithfulness, love, truth, and the responsibilities God has commanded.
That is why the church must become a place where victims can tell the truth without fearing that honesty will be punished.
Where women are protected.
Where men who experience abuse are not mocked or dismissed.
Where children are not told to normalize terror.
Where abusers are confronted with truth and accountability.
Where repentance is taken seriously enough that words alone are not accepted as proof.
Where pastors understand the limits of their expertise and work with trained professionals when needed.
Where biblical teaching about marriage is never separated from biblical teaching about justice, mercy, holiness, and the dignity of people made in God's image.
Because a church can preach against divorce every Sunday and still fail to confront the cruelty destroying marriages from within.
And when that happens, we have not defended God's design.
We have defended an appearance.
But Jesus has never been impressed by appearances.
He rebuked religious hypocrisy.
He exposed hearts that honored God with their lips while remaining far from Him.
He called His followers to truth.
And He taught that a tree is known by its fruit.
Not by its public reputation.
Not by the number of Bible verses it can recite.
Not by how spiritual it sounds during a prayer meeting.
By its fruit.
So if someone claims to love Jesus while terrorizing a spouse, that claim must be tested against the commands of Jesus.
If someone claims repentance while continuing threats and manipulation, those behaviors must be confronted.
And if someone claims to defend biblical marriage while refusing to protect the vulnerable, that position deserves serious examination in the light of Scripture.
Because the Gospel does not exist to make us more skilled at concealing sin.
It calls us out of darkness.
Into the light.
Into repentance.
Into grace.
Into transformation.
And that includes the abusive person reading this article.
Yes.
You, too.

If you recognize yourself in the controlling behavior, the threats, the intimidation, the manipulation, the use of Scripture to silence someone, do not hide behind the language of spiritual authority.
Do not demand that your spouse forgive you before you have faced what you have done.
Do not blame their reactions for your decisions.
Do not treat tears as payment for the damage.
Stop the abusive behavior.
Take responsibility.
Accept the boundaries and consequences necessary to protect those you have harmed.
Seek specialized professional help.
Submit to genuine accountability.
And turn to Jesus Christ in repentance.
The Gospel offers forgiveness to sinners who come to Christ.
But forgiveness is not permission to continue destroying someone.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
And restoration does not mean that the person you harmed must immediately trust you again.
The cross of Jesus Christ reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
Sin was not treated as a small inconvenience.
Christ bore its judgment.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who repent and believe.
That is why this message must never become merely an argument about divorce.
It is ultimately about the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
What does His Word actually teach?
What does genuine love look like?
What does repentance require?
How do we protect those who are suffering?
How do we pursue holiness without turning religion into a weapon?
And how do we tell the truth without losing sight of grace?
Maybe this article has made you uncomfortable.
Maybe you have used Malachi 2:16 without considering its context.
Maybe you have told someone to remain in danger because you feared encouraging divorce.
Maybe you were trying to protect marriage, but you now realize you failed to protect a person.
There is grace for you, too.
You can repent.
You can learn.
You can apologize.
You can become someone who listens before judging.
Someone who protects before pressuring.
Someone who takes Scripture seriously enough to read beyond a familiar phrase.
And perhaps, because you change, someone will finally feel safe enough to tell the truth.
Imagine that.
Imagine a church where a frightened person does not have to choose between being believed and being accepted.
Imagine a congregation where protecting victims is not treated as rebellion against marriage.
Imagine a Christian community where abusers cannot hide behind public spirituality.
Imagine children growing up understanding that love does not mean terror, submission does not mean accepting violence, and forgiveness does not mean surrendering every boundary.
Imagine a church that honors marriage so deeply that it refuses to excuse the evil that destroys it.
That is worth praying for.
That is worth working toward.
That is worth having difficult conversations about.
And it is worth sharing.
Not because every reader will agree with every theological conclusion.
But because someone on your Facebook friends list may be quietly wondering whether God has forgotten them.
Someone may be afraid to speak.
Someone may have been told that seeking safety is a sin.
Someone may need the courage to ask for help.
And if this has brought conviction, healing, or difficult questions to the surface, I want to invite you into a conversation that matters.
And if you have been part of a church culture that confused silence with holiness, perhaps your prayer today is simply:
"Jesus, forgive us. Teach us to love people the way You do."
Not as ammunition for another argument.
But as a reminder to return to the Scriptures, examine the context, and seek the truth when fear and religious pressure make everything confusing.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, Christians who have grown distant from God, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
Because everyone needs the truth of the Gospel.
And nobody should be told that Jesus is indifferent to their suffering.
There is also a deeper way to walk with this mission.
We want biblical nourishment to reach people who cannot afford expensive resources.
We want weary believers to find encouragement.
We want struggling families to encounter truth.
We want seekers to discover the Gospel.
We want disciples to grow beyond inspirational quotations into a deeper understanding of God's Word.
And we want this work to continue reaching people who may never walk into a church building but will read a message about Jesus on their phones in the middle of a desperate night.
And if you are struggling financially, please do not feel pressured to give.
The Gospel is not for sale.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
A conversation may help someone seek safety.
A prayer may strengthen someone who is exhausted.
And a faithful witness may point someone toward Jesus Christ.
That is why this work matters.
Not because we are building a name for ourselves.
But because the name of Jesus deserves to be proclaimed faithfully.
The one whose Bible is open.
The one who sings through tears.
The one who has been told that God cares more about preserving a marriage than about the suffering hidden inside it.
Imagine someone finally sitting beside that person and saying:
"I believe you."
"What happened to you matters."
"You do not deserve to be abused."
"We will help you find safety."
"We will seek God's wisdom together."
"And we will not use Scripture to silence you."
Imagine how different that moment could be.
Not because every difficult theological question has disappeared.
Not because divorce has suddenly become something to celebrate.
Not because marriage has lost its sacredness.
But because somebody has finally remembered that the God who created marriage also created the people within it.
People made in His image.
People for whom Christ came to save sinners.
People whose suffering is not invisible to Him.
And perhaps the most important question is not whether God hates divorce more than abuse.
Perhaps the question we should have been asking all along is this:
How did we ever become comfortable using God's hatred of covenant betrayal to excuse the very cruelty that betrays the covenant?
That question should trouble us.
It should lead us to repentance.
It should send us back to the Scriptures.
And it should bring us to the feet of Jesus Christ.
Because the Savior who calls us to holiness also calls us to mercy.
The Savior who honors covenant faithfulness also condemns oppression.
The Savior who commands forgiveness also commands truth.
And the Savior who died for sinners does not ask His people to pretend that sin is harmless.
There is hope for the wounded.
There is a call to repentance for the one doing harm.
There is responsibility for the church.
And there is redemption in Jesus Christ.
A shattered marriage may leave scars.
A broken trust may take years to process.
A painful chapter may never receive the earthly ending someone prayed for.
But the end of a marriage is not necessarily the end of a person's usefulness to God.
And the end of a painful chapter is not the end of Christ's power to redeem a life.
The hands that were nailed to the cross will never need your wounds to be hidden in order for His grace to be seen.
